subject.name: Biology
subject.description: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (Extended). Sample content covers every syllabus topic. The questions are original practice questions written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material.

topics.title: Characteristics and classification of living organisms
topics.summary: Characteristics of living organisms, the concept and uses of classification systems, features of organisms, dichotomous keys.

topics.title: Organisation of the organism
topics.summary: Cell structure, specialised cells, tissues and organs, size of specimens and magnification.

topics.title: Movement into and out of cells
topics.summary: Diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

topics.title: Biological molecules
topics.summary: Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, food tests and the structure of DNA.

topics.title: Enzymes
topics.summary: Enzyme action, specificity, and the effects of temperature and pH.

topics.title: Plant nutrition
topics.summary: Photosynthesis, leaf structure and mineral requirements.

topics.title: Human nutrition
topics.summary: Diet, digestive system, physical and chemical digestion, absorption.

topics.title: Transport in plants
topics.summary: Xylem and phloem, water uptake, transpiration and translocation.

topics.title: Transport in animals
topics.summary: Circulatory systems, the heart, blood vessels and blood.

topics.title: Diseases and immunity
topics.summary: Pathogens, transmission, defences and the immune response.

topics.title: Gas exchange in humans
topics.summary: Gas exchange surfaces, breathing and the effect of exercise.

topics.title: Respiration
topics.summary: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

topics.title: Excretion in humans
topics.summary: Excretory products, the kidney and the liver.

topics.title: Coordination and response
topics.summary: The nervous system, sense organs, hormones, homeostasis and tropic responses.

topics.title: Drugs
topics.summary: Medicinal drugs and antibiotics.

topics.title: Reproduction
topics.summary: Asexual and sexual reproduction in plants and humans, sex hormones, sexually transmitted infections.

topics.title: Inheritance
topics.summary: Chromosomes, genes and proteins, mitosis, meiosis and monohybrid inheritance.

topics.title: Variation and selection
topics.summary: Variation, adaptive features, natural and artificial selection.

topics.title: Organisms and their environment
topics.summary: Energy flow, food chains and webs, nutrient cycles and populations.

topics.title: Human influences on ecosystems
topics.summary: Food supply, habitat destruction, pollution and conservation.

topics.title: Biotechnology and genetic engineering
topics.summary: Biotechnology and genetic modification.

parts.prompt: Which characteristic of living organisms is described as 'the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism'?

markingPoints.text: C – respiration

parts.examinerComment: Candidates confused respiration with nutrition. Nutrition is taking in materials for energy, growth and development; respiration releases the energy.

parts.prompt: In the binomial system, which part of the name Panthera leo indicates the genus?

markingPoints.text: A – the first word is the genus

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: An organism has a body divided into three parts, three pairs of jointed legs and one pair of antennae. To which group does it belong?

markingPoints.text: C – insects

parts.examinerComment: Arachnids have four pairs of legs and no antennae, a frequent distractor.

parts.prompt: Which structure is found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell?

markingPoints.text: B – cell wall

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A cell is 0.05 mm long. In a drawing it is {d} mm long. What is the magnification of the drawing?
parts.examinerComment: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size, with both in the same units.

parts.prompt: Pieces of potato are placed in a concentrated sugar solution for one hour. What happens to the potato pieces?

options.text: They gain mass because water enters by osmosis.
They gain mass because sugar enters by diffusion.
They lose mass because water leaves by osmosis.
They lose mass because sugar leaves by active transport.

markingPoints.text: C – water moves from higher water potential (in the cells) to lower water potential (the solution)

parts.examinerComment: Answers should refer to water potential, not 'sugar concentration', when explaining osmosis.

parts.prompt: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from soil where the ion concentration is lower than inside the cell. Which process is used?

markingPoints.text: A – active transport moves ions against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A food sample turns biuret solution from blue to purple. Which nutrient is present?

markingPoints.text: B – protein

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should learn each food test with its positive result.

parts.prompt: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine?

markingPoints.text: D – thymine

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction decrease above the optimum temperature?

options.text: The enzyme molecules have less kinetic energy.
The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.
The substrate is used up more quickly.

markingPoints.text: B – denaturation changes the shape of the active site

parts.examinerComment: Enzymes are proteins, not living organisms, so they are denatured, not 'killed'.

questions.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the activity of amylase.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the substrate and the product of amylase.

markingPoints.text: substrate: starch
product: maltose / simple reducing sugar

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave 'glucose' as the product, which was not accepted.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the activity of amylase increases as the temperature increases from 20 °C to 35 °C.

markingPoints.text: molecules gain kinetic energy / move faster
more (successful) collisions between enzyme and substrate
more enzyme–substrate complexes formed (per unit time)

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers used the terms kinetic energy, collisions and enzyme–substrate complex. Vague references to enzymes 'working harder' gained no credit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the term osmosis.

markingPoints.text: net movement of water molecules
from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential
through a partially permeable membrane

parts.examinerComment: Definitions must refer to water molecules and a partially permeable membrane. 'Semi-permeable' was accepted.

parts.prompt: Which substance enters a leaf through the stomata and is used in photosynthesis?

markingPoints.text: A – carbon dioxide

parts.examinerComment: Oxygen was a common wrong answer. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis and leaves through the stomata.

parts.prompt: Why do plants need magnesium ions?

markingPoints.text: A – to make chlorophyll

parts.examinerComment: Candidates often confused magnesium with nitrate ions, which are needed to make amino acids.

parts.prompt: Where in the body is bile made?

markingPoints.text: B – liver

parts.examinerComment: Many chose the gall bladder. Bile is made in the liver and only stored in the gall bladder.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme digests protein in the stomach?

markingPoints.text: C – pepsin

parts.examinerComment: Trypsin also digests protein, but it works in the small intestine, not the stomach.

parts.prompt: Which tissue transports sucrose from the leaves to other parts of a plant?

markingPoints.text: C – phloem

parts.examinerComment: Xylem transports water and mineral ions; phloem transports sucrose and amino acids.

parts.prompt: Which condition increases the rate of transpiration?

markingPoints.text: B – high wind speed

parts.examinerComment: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

parts.prompt: Which blood vessel carries blood from the lungs to the heart?

markingPoints.text: C – pulmonary vein

parts.examinerComment: Remember that veins carry blood towards the heart, even when that blood is oxygenated.

parts.prompt: Which component of blood transports oxygen?

markingPoints.text: D – red blood cells

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What is a pathogen?

markingPoints.text: A – a disease-causing organism

parts.examinerComment: Well answered. Option C describes an antibody.

parts.prompt: How does a vaccine protect a person against a disease?

options.text: It contains antibiotics that kill the pathogen.
It contains antibodies that destroy the pathogen.
It contains antigens that stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells.
It contains white blood cells that engulf the pathogen.

markingPoints.text: C – It contains antigens that stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells.

parts.examinerComment: Option B describes passive immunity. A vaccine gives active immunity because the body makes its own antibodies.

parts.prompt: Which feature of the alveoli increases the rate of gas exchange?

markingPoints.text: D – thin walls

parts.examinerComment: A thin wall gives a short diffusion distance. Candidates should be able to list all the features of a gas exchange surface.

parts.prompt: What happens to the ribcage when the external intercostal muscles contract?

markingPoints.text: B – It moves up and out.

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What is produced by anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?

markingPoints.text: D – lactic acid

parts.examinerComment: Ethanol and carbon dioxide are produced by anaerobic respiration in yeast, not in muscles.

parts.prompt: In which part of a cell does most aerobic respiration take place?

markingPoints.text: B – mitochondria

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which organ breaks down excess amino acids to form urea?

markingPoints.text: C – liver

parts.examinerComment: Many chose the kidney. The kidney removes urea from the blood, but urea is made in the liver.

parts.prompt: Which substance is normally absent from the urine of a healthy person?

markingPoints.text: A – glucose

parts.examinerComment: Glucose is filtered out of the blood in the kidney, but all of it is normally reabsorbed.

parts.prompt: Which hormone lowers the concentration of glucose in the blood?

markingPoints.text: C – insulin

parts.examinerComment: Glucagon raises blood glucose. Learning the two hormones as a pair helps avoid confusion.

parts.prompt: Which part of the eye contains the light-sensitive receptor cells?

markingPoints.text: D – retina

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes a drug?

options.text: any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
any substance made by a doctor

markingPoints.text: B – any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body

parts.examinerComment: The syllabus definition is broad and includes medicines and recreational substances.

parts.prompt: Why should patients finish a full course of antibiotics?

options.text: to make the antibiotic work faster
to reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving and spreading
to stop the body making antibodies

markingPoints.text: C – to reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving and spreading

parts.examinerComment: Option B was a common error. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

parts.prompt: Where does fertilisation usually take place in humans?

markingPoints.text: B – oviduct

parts.examinerComment: Many chose the uterus. The embryo implants in the uterus after fertilisation in the oviduct.

parts.prompt: Which is a feature of insect-pollinated flowers?

markingPoints.text: C – large, brightly coloured petals

parts.examinerComment: The other three options are features of wind-pollinated flowers.

parts.prompt: What is an allele?

options.text: a length of DNA that codes for a protein
a change in a base sequence

markingPoints.text: B – a version of a gene

parts.examinerComment: Option A describes a gene. Candidates should use the terms gene and allele precisely.

parts.prompt: Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt) are crossed. T (tall) is dominant to t (short). What is the expected ratio of tall to short offspring?
parts.examinerComment: A Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt: three tall to one short.

parts.prompt: Which is an example of continuous variation in humans?

markingPoints.text: C – height

parts.examinerComment: Continuous variation has a range of values with no distinct categories.

parts.prompt: What is the original source of new alleles in a population?

markingPoints.text: B – mutation

parts.examinerComment: Sexual reproduction creates new combinations of alleles, but only mutation creates new alleles.

parts.prompt: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, which organism is the secondary consumer?

markingPoints.text: A – fox

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Why is the transfer of energy between trophic levels inefficient?

options.text: Energy is destroyed at each level.
Energy is lost to the environment, for example as heat from respiration.
Producers do not absorb any light energy.

markingPoints.text: B – Energy is lost to the environment, for example as heat from respiration.

parts.examinerComment: Option A was a common error. Energy is not destroyed; it is transferred to the environment.

parts.prompt: Which gas released by burning fossil fuels contributes most to the enhanced greenhouse effect?

markingPoints.text: A – carbon dioxide

parts.examinerComment: Sulfur dioxide was a common distractor. It causes acid rain, not the enhanced greenhouse effect.

parts.prompt: Fertiliser runs off farmland into a lake. What happens first?

markingPoints.text: A – Algae grow rapidly.

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should learn the sequence of eutrophication in order: algal growth, light blocked, plants die, decomposers respire, oxygen falls, fish die.

parts.prompt: Why are bacteria useful in biotechnology?

markingPoints.text: C – They reproduce rapidly.

parts.examinerComment: Other good reasons are that they have plasmids and there are few ethical concerns over their use.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme is used to cut DNA at specific sites in genetic modification?

markingPoints.text: D – restriction enzyme

parts.examinerComment: DNA ligase joins pieces of DNA; restriction enzymes cut them.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.

markingPoints.text: correct formulae: CO₂ and H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ and O₂
correctly balanced: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

parts.examinerComment: Light and chlorophyll may be written above the arrow. The most common error was balancing oxygen incorrectly.

parts.prompt: Explain how bile helps in the digestion of fats.

markingPoints.text: bile emulsifies fats
breaks fats into small droplets
increases the surface area for lipase to act on
bile neutralises stomach acid, giving the optimum pH for enzymes in the small intestine

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates wrote that bile digests fats. Bile is not an enzyme: it emulsifies fats so that lipase works faster.

parts.prompt: Define transpiration.

markingPoints.text: loss of water vapour from leaves
by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion of water vapour through the stomata

parts.examinerComment: Definitions that said only 'loss of water' did not gain full credit. The answer must refer to water vapour.

parts.prompt: A person's heart beats {b} times per minute. It pumps {v} cm³ of blood with each beat. Calculate the volume of blood pumped in one minute, in cm³.

markingPoints.text: volume = {b} × {v}
= {=b*v} cm³

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates multiplied correctly. A few divided, giving an answer smaller than one beat's volume.

parts.prompt: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat diseases caused by viruses.

markingPoints.text: antibiotics act on structures or processes found in bacteria, e.g. the cell wall
viruses do not have these structures / are not cells

parts.examinerComment: Answers saying viruses are 'too strong' or 'immune' gained no credit.

parts.prompt: State two differences between the composition of inspired air and expired air.

markingPoints.text: expired air contains more carbon dioxide
expired air contains less oxygen
expired air contains more water vapour

parts.examinerComment: Answers must be comparative: 'expired air has carbon dioxide' was not enough, since inspired air contains some too.

parts.prompt: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.

markingPoints.text: glucose + oxygen →
carbon dioxide + water

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates added 'energy' as a product. This was ignored, but energy is not a substance.

parts.prompt: Explain why glucose is not normally found in the urine of a healthy person.

markingPoints.text: glucose is filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus
all of it is reabsorbed (into the blood) in the tubule of the nephron

parts.examinerComment: Many said glucose is 'not filtered'. It is filtered, then reabsorbed.

parts.prompt: Describe the pathway of a nerve impulse in a reflex arc, from receptor to effector.

markingPoints.text: impulse travels from the receptor along a sensory neurone
to a relay neurone in the spinal cord / CNS
then along a motor neurone to the effector (muscle or gland)
impulses cross synapses between neurones

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers named all three types of neurone in the correct order.

parts.prompt: Explain how overuse of antibiotics can lead to populations of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

markingPoints.text: a random mutation makes some bacteria resistant
the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria
resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
passing on the resistance allele / gene

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should avoid saying bacteria 'become used to' or 'learn to resist' antibiotics.

parts.prompt: State two advantages of asexual reproduction for a plant.

markingPoints.text: only one parent is needed
it is faster
offspring are identical, so are well suited to the same environment
no pollinators are needed

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A plant with genotype Tt is crossed with a plant with genotype tt. T (tall) is dominant to t (short). What percentage of the offspring are expected to be short?

markingPoints.text: B1 for 50 (%)

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who drew a Punnett square were more successful.

parts.prompt: Explain the difference between natural selection and artificial selection.

markingPoints.text: in natural selection, the environment / selection pressures decide which individuals survive and reproduce
in artificial selection, humans choose individuals with desired features to breed

parts.examinerComment: Both processes needed to be described for full marks.

parts.prompt: A producer contains {E} kJ of energy. {p}% of this energy passes to the primary consumer. How much energy does the primary consumer receive, in kJ?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Describe how deforestation can increase the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

markingPoints.text: fewer trees photosynthesise, so less carbon dioxide is absorbed
burning trees releases carbon dioxide
decomposers break down dead wood and release carbon dioxide by respiration

parts.examinerComment: Many described only one process. Questions worth three marks usually need three distinct points.

parts.prompt: Explain why pectinase is used in the production of fruit juice.

markingPoints.text: pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls
so more juice is extracted / the juice is clearer

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

questions.stem: Fig. 1 shows the effect of temperature on the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.

figures.alt: Graph of rate of reaction against temperature for an enzyme: the rate rises from 5 at 0 °C to a peak of 90 at 40 °C, then falls to 0 at 60 °C.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the optimum temperature for this enzyme, in °C.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 40 °C

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the rate of reaction is zero at 60 °C.

markingPoints.text: the enzyme is denatured
the shape of the active site has changed
the substrate no longer fits / no enzyme–substrate complexes form

parts.examinerComment: Enzymes are not 'killed'.

questions.stem: Fig. 2 shows how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis at two concentrations of carbon dioxide.

figures.alt: Graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two carbon dioxide concentrations. Both lines rise together. At 0.04% carbon dioxide the rate levels off at 30 from light intensity 3; at 0.10% it levels off at 50 from light intensity 5.
figures.caption: Fig. 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the maximum rate of photosynthesis at 0.04% carbon dioxide, in arbitrary units.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 30

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at 0.04% carbon dioxide above a light intensity of 4 units. Explain how Fig. 2 shows this.

markingPoints.text: carbon dioxide concentration
increasing light intensity has no effect, but increasing carbon dioxide raises the rate

parts.examinerComment: Use evidence from both lines on the graph.

parts.prompt: Which list contains only characteristics shown by all living organisms?

markingPoints.text: C – movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth

parts.examinerComment: Breathing, digestion and photosynthesis are not carried out by all organisms. Candidates should learn the seven characteristics exactly.

parts.prompt: Why are the base sequences of DNA now used to help classify organisms?

options.text: Organisms with more similar base sequences share a more recent common ancestor.
Only organisms in the same kingdom contain DNA.
The base sequence of DNA is identical in all members of a genus.
DNA base sequences show the external features of an organism.

markingPoints.text: A – Organisms with more similar base sequences share a more recent common ancestor.

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers link similarity of DNA (or amino acid sequences in proteins) to how closely related organisms are through evolution.

parts.prompt: Which feature is found in mammals but not in birds?

markingPoints.text: B – fur and external ears (pinnae)

parts.examinerComment: Birds also have four-chambered hearts, lungs and a skeleton; fur, pinnae and mammary glands are distinctive mammal features.

parts.prompt: Which feature is shown by all prokaryotes?

markingPoints.text: A – cells with no nucleus

parts.examinerComment: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have circular DNA and plasmids but no nucleus. Many candidates wrongly gave cellulose cell walls, which are a plant feature.

parts.prompt: Which cell structure is the site of protein synthesis?

markingPoints.text: D – ribosome

parts.examinerComment: The nucleus holds the genes, but proteins are assembled on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

parts.prompt: Which sequence shows increasing levels of organisation?

markingPoints.text: B – cell → tissue → organ → organ system

parts.examinerComment: A tissue is a group of similar cells; an organ is made of several tissues; an organ system is a group of organs working together.

parts.prompt: Which specialised cell is correctly matched with its function?

options.text: ciliated cell – moves mucus in the trachea and bronchi
palisade mesophyll cell – absorption of mineral ions
red blood cell – production of antibodies

markingPoints.text: A – ciliated cell – moves mucus in the trachea and bronchi

parts.examinerComment: Each distractor gives a function belonging to a different cell type; learn one feature and one function for each specialised cell.

parts.prompt: Which change would increase the rate of diffusion of oxygen into a cell?

options.text: increasing the thickness of the cell surface
decreasing the surface area of the cell

markingPoints.text: C – increasing the concentration gradient

parts.examinerComment: Rate of diffusion increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature, a larger surface area and a shorter diffusion distance.

parts.prompt: A plant cell is placed in distilled water for one hour. What happens to the cell?

markingPoints.text: D – It becomes turgid.

parts.examinerComment: Water enters by osmosis and the cell wall resists further expansion, so plant cells do not burst. Many candidates confused plant and animal cells.

parts.prompt: Which statement about active transport is correct?

options.text: It moves particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration without energy.
It moves particles against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
It only moves water molecules through a partially permeable membrane.
It moves particles against a concentration gradient using energy from sunlight.

markingPoints.text: B – It moves particles against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

parts.examinerComment: Active transport uses carrier proteins in the membrane and energy released by respiration.

parts.prompt: Which chemical elements are present in fats?

markingPoints.text: A – carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only

parts.examinerComment: Fats, like carbohydrates, contain only C, H and O. Proteins also contain nitrogen.

parts.prompt: Which molecules are joined together to make a protein?

markingPoints.text: C – amino acids

parts.examinerComment: Proteins are chains of amino acids; fats are made from fatty acids and glycerol; starch from glucose.

parts.prompt: Which test shows that a solution contains a reducing sugar?

options.text: Add iodine solution; it turns blue-black.
Add Benedict's solution and heat; it turns from blue to brick-red.
Shake with ethanol then add water; a white emulsion forms.
Add biuret solution; it turns from blue to purple.

markingPoints.text: B – Add Benedict's solution and heat; it turns from blue to brick-red.

parts.examinerComment: Benedict's solution must be heated in a water bath. The colour change can be green, yellow, orange or brick-red depending on concentration.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes the structure of a DNA molecule?

options.text: one strand folded into a ball with bases on the outside
two strands coiled into a double helix, with A pairing with C and G with T
two strands coiled into a double helix, with A pairing with T and C with G
three strands twisted together, held by bonds between sugars

markingPoints.text: C – two strands coiled into a double helix, with A pairing with T and C with G

parts.examinerComment: Each strand carries a sequence of bases; bonds between complementary bases (A–T, C–G) hold the two strands together.

parts.prompt: What is an enzyme?

options.text: a carbohydrate that speeds up digestion
a protein that functions as a biological catalyst
a fat that is used up in chemical reactions

markingPoints.text: B – a protein that functions as a biological catalyst

parts.examinerComment: Enzymes are proteins and are not used up in the reactions they catalyse.

parts.prompt: The enzyme pepsin works best at pH 2. Some pepsin is placed in a solution at pH 9. Why does it stop working?

options.text: The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.
The enzyme molecules move too slowly.

markingPoints.text: C – The shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.

parts.examinerComment: Enzymes are molecules, not living things, so they cannot be 'killed'. An unsuitable pH denatures the enzyme.

parts.prompt: When testing a leaf for starch, why is the leaf placed in hot ethanol?

options.text: to break down the starch to glucose

markingPoints.text: D – to remove the chlorophyll

parts.examinerComment: Removing the green colour lets the blue-black colour of iodine solution be seen. Boiling in water is the step that kills the cells.

parts.prompt: Why do plants need nitrate ions?

markingPoints.text: A – to make amino acids

parts.examinerComment: Nitrate ions supply nitrogen for amino acids (and therefore proteins). Magnesium is needed for chlorophyll.

parts.prompt: A child has soft, weak bones. Which nutrient is most likely missing from the diet?

markingPoints.text: C – vitamin D

parts.examinerComment: Vitamin D (with calcium) is needed for strong bones; lack of it causes rickets. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

parts.prompt: What are the functions of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?

options.text: to digest fats and neutralise bile
to kill pathogens in food and give a low pH for pepsin
to emulsify fats and absorb water
to digest starch and kill pathogens

markingPoints.text: B – to kill pathogens in food and give a low pH for pepsin

parts.examinerComment: Hydrochloric acid does not digest food itself; it provides the acid pH that is optimum for protease in the stomach.

parts.prompt: Which organ absorbs most of the water from food and drink?

markingPoints.text: A – small intestine

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates choose the colon. Most water is absorbed in the small intestine; the colon absorbs most of what remains.

parts.prompt: What is the product of the digestion of starch by amylase?

markingPoints.text: D – maltose

parts.examinerComment: Amylase breaks starch into maltose; maltase on the membranes of the small intestine epithelium then breaks maltose into glucose.

parts.prompt: Which sequence shows the pathway taken by water through a plant?

options.text: root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
root hair cell → phloem → xylem → mesophyll cells
xylem → root hair cell → mesophyll cells → stomata
root cortex cells → root hair cell → phloem → mesophyll cells

markingPoints.text: A – root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells

parts.examinerComment: Water travels in the xylem, not the phloem. It evaporates from mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata.

parts.prompt: Which feature of xylem vessels helps them to transport water?

options.text: They are living cells with a large vacuole.
They are hollow tubes with no cross walls, strengthened with lignin.
They have sieve plates between cells.

markingPoints.text: C – They are hollow tubes with no cross walls, strengthened with lignin.

parts.examinerComment: Sieve plates are found in phloem. Xylem vessels are dead, hollow and continuous.

parts.prompt: Which part of a plant is acting as a sink for sucrose?

options.text: a mature leaf in bright light
a xylem vessel in the stem

markingPoints.text: B – a fruit that is developing

parts.examinerComment: A sink is where sucrose is used or stored, such as growing regions, developing fruits and storage organs.

parts.prompt: What is meant by a double circulation?

options.text: Blood flows through the heart twice in each complete circuit of the body.
Blood flows in arteries and veins.
Blood is pumped twice by each ventricle in every beat.

markingPoints.text: A – Blood flows through the heart twice in each complete circuit of the body.

parts.examinerComment: In a double circulation one circuit goes to the lungs and the other to the rest of the body.

parts.prompt: Why is the muscle wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?

options.text: It pumps blood to the lungs.
It holds a larger volume of blood.
It pumps blood at a higher pressure around the whole body.

markingPoints.text: C – It pumps blood at a higher pressure around the whole body.

parts.examinerComment: Both ventricles hold similar volumes. The left ventricle must generate a higher pressure to send blood around the systemic circulation.

parts.prompt: What is the function of the valves in the heart?

options.text: to separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
to supply the heart muscle with oxygen

markingPoints.text: B – to prevent backflow of blood

parts.examinerComment: The septum separates the two sides; the coronary arteries supply the heart muscle.

parts.prompt: Which type of blood cell produces antibodies?

markingPoints.text: A – lymphocyte

parts.examinerComment: Phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies.

parts.prompt: How is cholera usually transmitted?

options.text: in droplets from coughs and sneezes

markingPoints.text: C – in water contaminated with faeces

parts.examinerComment: Treatment of sewage and a clean water supply prevent the spread of cholera.

parts.prompt: A baby receives antibodies from its mother in breast milk. What type of immunity is this?

markingPoints.text: B – passive immunity

parts.examinerComment: The baby has not made the antibodies itself, so no memory cells form and the protection is short-term.

parts.prompt: Which is a chemical barrier against pathogens?

markingPoints.text: C – stomach acid

parts.examinerComment: Skin and nose hairs are mechanical barriers; phagocytes are cells, not barriers.

parts.prompt: Which sequence shows the path of air into the lungs?

markingPoints.text: A – trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli

parts.examinerComment: The trachea divides into two bronchi, which branch into many bronchioles ending in alveoli.

parts.prompt: During exercise, what causes the rate and depth of breathing to increase?

options.text: a fall in the carbon dioxide concentration of the blood
an increase in the carbon dioxide concentration of the blood, detected by the brain
an increase in the oxygen concentration of the blood
a decrease in the temperature of the lungs

markingPoints.text: B – an increase in the carbon dioxide concentration of the blood, detected by the brain

parts.examinerComment: Extra respiration in muscles releases more carbon dioxide. The brain detects the rise and increases the breathing rate and depth.

parts.prompt: What is the function of goblet cells in the trachea?

options.text: to produce mucus that traps pathogens and particles

markingPoints.text: C – to produce mucus that traps pathogens and particles

parts.examinerComment: Ciliated cells move the mucus; cartilage keeps the trachea open.

parts.prompt: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?

markingPoints.text: A – ethanol and carbon dioxide

parts.examinerComment: Lactic acid is produced by anaerobic respiration in muscle cells, not in yeast.

parts.prompt: Which process in the human body does not use energy released by respiration?

options.text: diffusion of oxygen into red blood cells

markingPoints.text: C – diffusion of oxygen into red blood cells

parts.examinerComment: Diffusion is a passive process. Energy from respiration is used for muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses and keeping body temperature constant.

parts.prompt: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration?

options.text: Glucose is only partly broken down.
Anaerobic respiration happens only in mitochondria.
Oxygen is used up too quickly.

markingPoints.text: B – Glucose is only partly broken down.

parts.examinerComment: The products (lactic acid or ethanol) still contain much of the chemical energy from glucose.

parts.prompt: What is deamination?

options.text: the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea
the filtration of blood in the kidney
the breakdown of glucose to release energy
the removal of water from urine

markingPoints.text: A – the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids to form urea

parts.examinerComment: Deamination happens in the liver; the urea formed is carried in the blood plasma to the kidneys.

parts.prompt: Which structure carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?

markingPoints.text: C – ureter

parts.examinerComment: Candidates often confuse the ureter (kidney to bladder) with the urethra (bladder to outside).

parts.prompt: In which part of a nephron is blood filtered?

markingPoints.text: C – the glomerulus

parts.examinerComment: High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules into the Bowman's capsule (renal capsule).

parts.prompt: A person walks from a dark room into bright sunlight. What happens in the iris?

options.text: Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, so the pupil gets smaller.
Circular muscles relax and radial muscles contract, so the pupil gets smaller.
Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, so the pupil gets larger.
Both sets of muscles contract, so the pupil gets larger.

markingPoints.text: A – Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, so the pupil gets smaller.

parts.examinerComment: The two muscle sets are antagonistic: when one contracts the other relaxes.

parts.prompt: A shoot is lit from one side. Why does it bend towards the light?

options.text: Auxin is destroyed on the shaded side.
Auxin collects on the shaded side and cells there elongate more.
Auxin collects on the lit side and cells there elongate more.
Cells on the lit side divide faster.

markingPoints.text: B – Auxin collects on the shaded side and cells there elongate more.

parts.examinerComment: Auxin stimulates cell elongation in shoots. More elongation on the shaded side bends the shoot towards the light.

parts.prompt: How does an impulse pass across a synapse?

options.text: Electrical impulses jump across the gap.
Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors.
Neurotransmitter is actively transported along the axon.

markingPoints.text: B – Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors.

parts.examinerComment: Synapses ensure impulses travel in one direction only, because receptors are only on the next neurone.

parts.prompt: Which effects are caused by adrenaline?

options.text: decreased heart rate and increased pupil diameter
increased heart rate and decreased breathing rate
decreased blood glucose and decreased heart rate
increased heart rate, breathing rate and pupil diameter

markingPoints.text: D – increased heart rate, breathing rate and pupil diameter

parts.examinerComment: Adrenaline prepares the body for 'fight or flight', including raising blood glucose concentration.

parts.prompt: Which disease can be treated with antibiotics?

markingPoints.text: B – cholera

parts.examinerComment: Cholera is caused by a bacterium. The others are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not affect.

parts.prompt: Why can some antibiotics kill bacteria without harming human cells?

options.text: Human cells are too large to be affected.
The antibiotics act on structures, such as the cell wall, that human cells do not have.
Human cells contain antibodies that destroy the antibiotic.
Antibiotics only work outside the body.

markingPoints.text: B – The antibiotics act on structures, such as the cell wall, that human cells do not have.

parts.examinerComment: Antibiotics target processes or structures found in bacteria but not in human cells.

parts.prompt: Which action helps to reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA?

options.text: using antibiotics to treat viral infections
stopping a course of antibiotics as soon as symptoms go
using antibiotics only when they are essential
giving antibiotics to all healthy farm animals

markingPoints.text: C – using antibiotics only when they are essential

parts.examinerComment: Each use of an antibiotic selects for resistant bacteria, so limiting their use slows the spread of resistance.

parts.prompt: What is the function of the anther in a flower?

markingPoints.text: B – to produce pollen

parts.examinerComment: The stigma receives pollen; ovules are inside the ovary.

parts.prompt: What is a function of the placenta?

options.text: to let maternal blood mix with fetal blood
to protect the fetus from mechanical shocks
to exchange dissolved nutrients, gases and wastes between mother and fetus

markingPoints.text: C – to exchange dissolved nutrients, gases and wastes between mother and fetus

parts.examinerComment: Maternal and fetal blood do not mix. Amniotic fluid protects the fetus from shocks.

parts.prompt: Which hormone maintains the lining of the uterus after ovulation?

markingPoints.text: D – progesterone

parts.examinerComment: FSH and LH are made by the pituitary gland and control egg development and ovulation; progesterone maintains the uterus lining.

parts.prompt: Which method reduces the spread of HIV?

markingPoints.text: A – using condoms during sexual intercourse

parts.examinerComment: HIV is spread in body fluids, such as during sexual intercourse or by sharing needles.

parts.prompt: How many chromosomes are present in a human egg cell?
parts.examinerComment: Gametes are haploid, with one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs.

parts.prompt: Which statement about mitosis is correct?

options.text: It produces four genetically different cells.
It only takes place in the ovaries and testes.

markingPoints.text: C – It produces genetically identical cells.

parts.examinerComment: Mitosis is used for growth, repair of tissues, replacement of cells and asexual reproduction.

parts.prompt: A man with genotype IᴬIᴼ and a woman with genotype IᴮIᴼ have a child. What is the probability that the child has blood group O?
parts.examinerComment: Only the IᴼIᴼ combination gives group O; it is one of four equally likely combinations.

parts.prompt: Which human feature shows discontinuous variation?

markingPoints.text: C – ABO blood group

parts.examinerComment: Discontinuous variation falls into distinct groups with no intermediates, and is usually caused by genes alone.

parts.prompt: Which factor increases the rate of mutation?

markingPoints.text: A – ionising radiation

parts.examinerComment: Ionising radiation and some chemicals increase the rate of mutation.

parts.prompt: Which adaptive features are found in a xerophyte?

options.text: thin cuticle and many stomata on the upper surface
large air spaces in stems and leaves
thick waxy cuticle and sunken stomata
wide, thin leaves floating on water

markingPoints.text: C – thick waxy cuticle and sunken stomata

parts.examinerComment: The other options describe hydrophytes or features that would increase water loss.

parts.prompt: What is the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle?

options.text: They absorb carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
They release carbon dioxide by respiration.
They turn carbon dioxide into fossil fuels.
They release carbon dioxide by combustion.

markingPoints.text: B – They release carbon dioxide by respiration.

parts.examinerComment: Decomposers feed on dead organic matter and release carbon dioxide when they respire.

parts.prompt: What do nitrogen-fixing bacteria do?

options.text: convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds such as ammonium ions

markingPoints.text: A – convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds such as ammonium ions

parts.examinerComment: Converting nitrates into nitrogen gas is denitrification; converting proteins to ammonium is decomposition.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes the stationary phase of a population growth curve?

options.text: The birth rate is much higher than the death rate.
The birth rate and death rate are approximately equal.
The death rate is much higher than the birth rate.

markingPoints.text: B – The birth rate and death rate are approximately equal.

parts.examinerComment: Limiting factors such as food, space or predators stop the population increasing.

parts.prompt: Why can a pyramid of numbers have a narrow base, unlike a pyramid of biomass?

options.text: Producers contain less energy than consumers.
One large producer, such as a tree, can feed many consumers.
Energy is gained at each trophic level.
Consumers are always larger than producers.

markingPoints.text: B – One large producer, such as a tree, can feed many consumers.

parts.examinerComment: A pyramid of biomass is almost always a true pyramid because biomass decreases at each level.

parts.prompt: What is a negative effect of growing crops as large monocultures?

markingPoints.text: B – reduced biodiversity

parts.examinerComment: Monocultures remove habitats for many species and pests can spread quickly, so more pesticide is often used.

parts.prompt: During eutrophication, why does the oxygen concentration of the water fall?

options.text: Decomposers increase and use oxygen in aerobic respiration as they break down dead plants.

markingPoints.text: C – Decomposers increase and use oxygen in aerobic respiration as they break down dead plants.

parts.examinerComment: Light is blocked by surface algae, so plants below die; decomposition by bacteria then uses up dissolved oxygen.

parts.prompt: Which method helps to make fishing sustainable?

options.text: using nets with very small mesh
setting quotas on the mass of fish caught

markingPoints.text: B – setting quotas on the mass of fish caught

parts.examinerComment: Quotas, larger mesh sizes and closed seasons allow fish populations to replace themselves.

parts.prompt: Which human activity is a major source of methane?

markingPoints.text: B – rearing cattle

parts.examinerComment: Methane is released by cattle and from rice fields and landfill sites. Burning coal mainly releases carbon dioxide.

parts.prompt: Why is yeast added to bread dough?

options.text: It produces lactic acid that flavours the bread.
It produces carbon dioxide that makes the dough rise.
It kills bacteria in the flour.

markingPoints.text: B – It produces carbon dioxide that makes the dough rise.

parts.examinerComment: Yeast respires anaerobically, producing carbon dioxide; the ethanol evaporates during baking.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme joins a gene into a plasmid during genetic modification?

markingPoints.text: D – DNA ligase

parts.examinerComment: Restriction enzymes cut DNA; DNA ligase joins the sticky ends.

parts.prompt: What are 'sticky ends' in genetic modification?

options.text: short lengths of unpaired, complementary bases left after DNA is cut

markingPoints.text: A – short lengths of unpaired, complementary bases left after DNA is cut

parts.examinerComment: Using the same restriction enzyme on both pieces of DNA gives complementary sticky ends that can pair up.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme is used to produce milk suitable for people who are lactose intolerant?

markingPoints.text: A – lactase

parts.examinerComment: Lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose.

parts.prompt:
Four animals have these features:
• P – six legs, wings
• Q – eight legs, no wings
• R – six legs, no wings
• S – more than ten pairs of legs
Construct a dichotomous key to identify the four animals.

markingPoints.text: first question splits the animals into two groups, e.g. more than 8 legs? (S) / 8 or fewer
question separating Q (eight legs) from the six-legged animals
question about wings separating P from R
each question has two paired, opposite answers that lead to a name or the next question
all four animals correctly identified at the end of the key

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used numbered paired statements based on visible features. Weaker answers asked about features not given, or wrote questions with more than two outcomes.

parts.prompt: Explain why viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.

markingPoints.text: viruses are not made of cells / have no cell structure
they consist only of genetic material inside a protein coat
they do not show all the characteristics of living organisms / can only reproduce inside host cells

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates simply said viruses are 'not alive' without explaining why.

parts.prompt: State the term for a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.

markingPoints.text: species

parts.examinerComment: Answers such as 'genus' or 'population' were not accepted.

questions.stem: A student measures a red blood cell in a photomicrograph.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The image of the cell is {I} mm wide. The magnification of the photomicrograph is ×{M}. Calculate the actual width of the cell in micrometres (µm).

markingPoints.text: actual size = image size ÷ magnification

parts.examinerComment: The most common error was not converting millimetres to micrometres (1 mm = 1000 µm).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the functions of the mitochondria and the ribosomes in a cell.

markingPoints.text: mitochondria: site of (aerobic) respiration / release energy
ribosomes: protein synthesis

parts.examinerComment: 'Mitochondria make energy' was not accepted: energy is released, not made.

parts.prompt: A student draws a pollen grain. The drawing is {d} mm across. The actual pollen grain is {a} µm across. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

markingPoints.text: magnification = {=d*1000} ÷ {a} = ×{=d*1000/a}

parts.examinerComment: Magnification has no units. Both measurements must be in the same unit before dividing.

parts.prompt: Name the cell structure that controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

markingPoints.text: cell membrane

parts.examinerComment: 'Cell wall' was a common incorrect answer; the cell wall is fully permeable.

parts.prompt: Explain how a root hair cell is adapted for its function.

markingPoints.text: long extension / root hair gives a large surface area
for absorption of water and mineral ions
no chloroplasts as it is underground / many mitochondria for active transport

parts.examinerComment: Answers should link each feature to the function it helps.

questions.stem: A student cuts cylinders from a potato, weighs them and places them in a concentrated salt solution for 30 minutes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The total mass of the cylinders decreased from {m0} g to {m1} g. Calculate the percentage decrease in mass.

markingPoints.text: decrease = {m0} − {m1} = {=round(m0-m1, 1)} g

parts.examinerComment: Divide the change by the original mass, not the final mass.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the decrease in mass of the cylinders.

markingPoints.text: the salt solution has a lower water potential than the potato cells
water leaves the cells by osmosis
through the partially permeable (cell) membrane
from a higher to a lower water potential / down a water potential gradient

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used the term water potential correctly. Answers referring to salt moving into the cells did not gain credit.

parts.prompt: Red blood cells placed in distilled water burst, but plant cells in distilled water do not. Explain this difference.

markingPoints.text: water enters both types of cell by osmosis
red blood cells have no cell wall, so the membrane stretches until it bursts
plant cells have a cell wall that resists expansion / pressure
so plant cells become turgid

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates stated that plant cells have a cell wall but did not explain how the wall prevents bursting.

parts.prompt: Describe how a student could test a sample of food for the presence of fat.

markingPoints.text: mix / shake the food with ethanol
pour the liquid into (cold) water
a cloudy white emulsion shows fat is present

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who described the Sudan III or Benedict's test did not gain credit; the ethanol emulsion test is required.

parts.prompt: Name the carbohydrate made of many glucose molecules that is stored in plant cells.

markingPoints.text: starch

parts.examinerComment: Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate in animals; cellulose forms cell walls.

questions.stem: Part of one strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence ATTGCAC.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the base sequence of the corresponding part of the complementary strand.
acceptedAnswers: T A A C G T G

markingPoints.text: TAACGTG

parts.examinerComment: A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Some candidates wrote U, which is not found in DNA.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In another DNA molecule, {A}% of the bases are adenine. Calculate the percentage of the bases that are guanine.

markingPoints.text: thymine is also {A}% (A pairs with T)

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot that thymine must equal adenine, and gave 100 − {A} or similar.

parts.prompt: Explain why an enzyme can only catalyse one type of reaction.

markingPoints.text: the active site has a specific shape
only one substrate is complementary to the active site
enzyme–substrate complex forms
other molecules do not fit the active site

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used 'complementary' rather than 'the same shape'.

parts.prompt: The enzyme catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide to release oxygen. In one experiment, {v} cm³ of oxygen was collected in {t} seconds. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute.

markingPoints.text: {v} ÷ {t} = {=v/t} cm³ per second
× 60 = {=v/t*60} cm³ per minute

parts.examinerComment: Read the units asked for carefully: the time was given in seconds but the rate is per minute.

parts.prompt: Describe an experiment using a variegated leaf (with green and white areas) to show that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

markingPoints.text: destarch the plant by keeping it in the dark for 48 hours
then place it in light for several hours
test the leaf for starch: boil in water, then in ethanol, then add iodine solution
green areas turn blue-black / white areas stay orange-brown
so starch is only made where chlorophyll is present

parts.examinerComment: The destarching step was often omitted, which means the starch could have been made before the experiment.

questions.stem: A student investigates the rate of photosynthesis of a piece of pondweed by counting the bubbles of gas it releases.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The student counts {n} bubbles in {t} minutes. Calculate the rate of bubble production in bubbles per minute.

markingPoints.text: {n} ÷ {t} = {=n/t} bubbles per minute

parts.examinerComment: Answers to three significant figures were accepted.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The student moves a lamp closer to the pondweed and the rate of bubble production increases. Explain why.

markingPoints.text: light intensity increases
light intensity is the limiting factor
more energy is available / absorbed by chlorophyll for photosynthesis

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers identified light intensity as the limiting factor.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Suggest two variables that should be kept constant during this investigation.

markingPoints.text: temperature (of the water)
carbon dioxide concentration / amount of hydrogencarbonate
same piece / species / length of pondweed
time allowed to adjust before counting

parts.examinerComment: Light intensity was not accepted because it is the independent variable.

parts.prompt: Explain how the palisade mesophyll cells of a leaf are adapted for photosynthesis.

markingPoints.text: contain many chloroplasts
to absorb light energy
found near the upper surface of the leaf, where light is brightest
tall cells packed closely together so many fit near the surface

parts.examinerComment: Answers should link each feature to how it helps the cell trap light.

parts.prompt: Describe how a student could investigate the effect of pH on the activity of amylase, using starch and iodine solution.

markingPoints.text: mix amylase and starch solution in buffers of different pH
keep temperature constant using a water bath
take samples at regular intervals, e.g. every 30 s, and add to iodine solution on a spotting tile
record the time until iodine no longer turns blue-black / stays orange-brown
same volumes / concentrations of amylase and starch at each pH
shortest time shows the optimum pH

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained how the end point was identified and controlled the temperature.

parts.prompt: Explain how the structure of villi increases the rate of absorption of digested food.

markingPoints.text: villi (and microvilli) give a large surface area
wall is one cell thick / short diffusion distance
good blood supply / many capillaries maintains a concentration gradient
lacteal absorbs fatty acids and glycerol
many mitochondria in epithelial cells for active transport

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to link each feature to faster absorption, not just list features.

parts.prompt: Explain why chewing food increases the rate of chemical digestion.

markingPoints.text: breaks food into smaller pieces
increases surface area
for enzymes to act on

parts.examinerComment: Chewing is physical digestion: it does not break chemical bonds.

parts.prompt: A food label states that 100 g of a breakfast cereal contains {e} kJ of energy. A student eats {m} g of the cereal. Calculate the energy the student obtains, in kJ.
parts.examinerComment: Most candidates scaled correctly from 100 g.

questions.stem: A student uses a potometer to measure water uptake by a leafy shoot.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The air bubble moves {d} mm along the capillary tube in {t} minutes. The cross-sectional area of the capillary tube is {A} mm². Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ per minute.

markingPoints.text: volume = {d} × {A} = {=d*A} mm³
÷ {t} min
= {=d*A/t} mm³ per minute

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates forgot to multiply by the cross-sectional area and gave a distance per minute.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the rate of water uptake increases when the temperature increases.

markingPoints.text: water molecules have more kinetic energy
faster evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces
faster diffusion of water vapour out through stomata
so transpiration rate increases and more water is pulled up

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked the increased transpiration to water uptake by the shoot.

parts.prompt: Explain how water moves up the xylem from the roots to the leaves.

markingPoints.text: water evaporates from mesophyll cells and diffuses out through stomata (transpiration)
this creates a transpiration pull / tension
water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion)
so a continuous column of water is pulled up the xylem

parts.examinerComment: 'Water is sucked up' without reference to evaporation and cohesion gained little credit.

parts.prompt: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function.

markingPoints.text: thick muscular wall to withstand high pressure
elastic tissue stretches and recoils
to even out / maintain blood pressure / flow
narrow lumen maintains high pressure

parts.examinerComment: Answers should describe a feature and then explain its purpose.

parts.prompt: Name the blood vessels that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.

markingPoints.text: coronary arteries

parts.examinerComment: Blood inside the chambers does not supply the heart muscle; 'aorta' was a common incorrect answer.

parts.prompt: State three risk factors for coronary heart disease.

markingPoints.text: diet high in saturated fat
lack of exercise
smoking
stress
genetic predisposition
age / being male

parts.examinerComment: Vague answers such as 'unhealthy lifestyle' were not credited.

parts.prompt: Explain how the cholera bacterium causes diarrhoea and dehydration.

markingPoints.text: bacterium produces a toxin
toxin causes secretion of chloride ions into the small intestine
this lowers the water potential of the gut contents
water moves into the gut by osmosis
water is lost in faeces / diarrhoea, causing loss of water and ions from the blood

parts.examinerComment: Only the strongest answers referred to chloride ions and water potential.

parts.prompt: Explain why antibodies made against the measles virus do not protect a person against the influenza virus.

markingPoints.text: antibodies are specific
antibody shape is complementary to one antigen only
influenza virus has different antigens

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should refer to antigens, not to the virus 'not fitting'.

parts.prompt: Explain why a person who has been vaccinated is unlikely to become ill if later infected with the same pathogen.

markingPoints.text: memory cells were produced after vaccination
on infection, memory cells recognise the antigen
antibodies are produced more quickly
and in larger quantities, so pathogen destroyed before symptoms

parts.examinerComment: This is active immunity: it is long-term because memory cells remain.

questions.stem: A student measures their breathing rate at rest and immediately after exercise.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: At rest the breathing rate was {r} breaths per minute. Immediately after exercise it was {e} breaths per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in breathing rate.

markingPoints.text: increase = {e} − {r} = {=e-r}

parts.examinerComment: Divide by the resting value, which is the original value.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how limewater could be used to show that expired air contains more carbon dioxide than inspired air.

markingPoints.text: breathe out through one tube of limewater and draw air in through another tube
limewater turns milky / cloudy faster with expired air
same volume of limewater in each tube

parts.examinerComment: A fair test needs the same volume of limewater; stronger answers compared the time taken to turn cloudy.

parts.prompt: Describe the roles of the muscles in breathing out forcefully, for example during exercise.

markingPoints.text: internal intercostal muscles contract
ribcage moves down and in
diaphragm relaxes and moves up / becomes dome-shaped
volume of thorax decreases, pressure increases, air forced out

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates confused the roles of the internal and external intercostal muscles.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration.

markingPoints.text: correct formulae: C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
balanced: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O

parts.examinerComment: Energy is not a substance and should not be written as a product in a symbol equation.

parts.prompt: After a sprint, an athlete continues to breathe deeply and quickly. Explain why.

markingPoints.text: anaerobic respiration during sprint produced lactic acid
oxygen debt
lactic acid transported in the blood to the liver
extra oxygen needed for aerobic respiration of lactic acid / to break it down
fast heart rate continues to transport lactic acid

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers described how the oxygen debt is removed, not just that it exists.

parts.prompt: Yeast in a sugar solution produced {a} bubbles of carbon dioxide per minute at 20 °C and {b} bubbles per minute at 30 °C. Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of respiration.

markingPoints.text: increase = {b} − {a} = {=b-a}

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates divided by the final value instead of the initial value.

parts.prompt: Explain what happens to excess amino acids in the body.

markingPoints.text: amino acids cannot be stored
deaminated in the liver
nitrogen-containing part removed / converted to urea
urea carried in the blood plasma to the kidneys and excreted in urine

parts.examinerComment: Answers stating that the kidneys make urea were not credited.

parts.prompt: The kidneys of a person filter {f} dm³ of fluid from the blood each day. The person produces {u} dm³ of urine each day. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed.

markingPoints.text: reabsorbed = {f} − {u} = {=round(f-u, 1)} dm³

parts.examinerComment: Answers to three significant figures were accepted; rounding to 100% was not.

parts.prompt: Name the excretory product removed from the body by the lungs.

markingPoints.text: carbon dioxide

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates answered correctly. Carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration, so its removal is excretion. Answers of 'oxygen' or 'air' gained no credit.

parts.prompt: Describe how the body responds to lower its temperature when it becomes too hot.

markingPoints.text: hypothalamus / brain detects increase in temperature
vasodilation of arterioles near the skin surface
more blood flows near the skin, so more heat is lost by radiation
sweat glands produce more sweat
evaporation of sweat removes heat

parts.examinerComment: Blood vessels do not move up and down in the skin; 'veins dilate' was also not credited.

parts.prompt: Compare nervous control with hormonal control in the body.

markingPoints.text: nervous uses electrical impulses; hormonal uses chemicals in the blood
nervous is faster
nervous effects are shorter-lasting
nervous acts on a specific area; hormones can affect several target organs

parts.examinerComment: A comparison needs both sides stated, or comparative words such as 'faster'.

parts.prompt: Name the type of neurone that passes impulses from a sensory neurone to a motor neurone in the spinal cord.

markingPoints.text: relay neurone

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates answered this correctly.

parts.prompt: Give the name of a strain of bacteria that is resistant to many antibiotics and is a problem in hospitals.

markingPoints.text: MRSA

parts.examinerComment: The abbreviation was accepted.

parts.prompt: Suggest why antibiotic-resistant bacteria are more common in hospitals than in other places.

markingPoints.text: antibiotics are used more often in hospitals
this kills non-resistant bacteria / selects resistant bacteria
resistant bacteria survive, reproduce and pass on resistance
many patients are close together / have weak immune systems, so bacteria spread easily

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to refer to selection, not to bacteria 'becoming immune'.

parts.prompt: One antibiotic-resistant bacterium survives a course of antibiotics. It divides into two every 20 minutes. Calculate how many bacteria there would be after {t} minutes, assuming none die.

markingPoints.text: number of divisions = {t} ÷ 20 = {=t/20}
2 to the power {=t/20} = {=2^(t/20)}

parts.examinerComment: A common error was to multiply 2 by the number of divisions instead of doubling repeatedly.

parts.prompt: Describe three ways in which wind-pollinated flowers differ from insect-pollinated flowers.

markingPoints.text: small / dull petals (not brightly coloured)
no scent or nectar
anthers hang outside the flower
large, feathery stigmas outside the flower
large amounts of small, light, smooth pollen

parts.examinerComment: Answers should describe the wind-pollinated flower, not just state 'the opposite'.

parts.prompt: Explain how a sperm cell is adapted for its function.

markingPoints.text: flagellum for swimming
many mitochondria release energy for movement
acrosome contains enzymes to digest the jelly coat of the egg
haploid nucleus

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked each feature to its role in reaching or fertilising the egg.

parts.prompt: Name the part of a flower that receives pollen during pollination.

markingPoints.text: stigma

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates gave 'ovary' or 'style'.

parts.prompt: In guinea pigs, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant to the allele for white fur (b). Explain how a test cross could show whether a black guinea pig is homozygous or heterozygous.

markingPoints.text: cross the black guinea pig with a white (bb) guinea pig
if all offspring are black, the parent is BB
if about half are white, the parent is Bb
white offspring must receive b from both parents

parts.examinerComment: Genetic diagrams were helpful when clearly labelled with parent genotypes and gametes.

parts.prompt: Describe how a gene controls the production of a protein.

markingPoints.text: the sequence of bases in DNA codes for the sequence of amino acids
a copy of the gene is made as mRNA in the nucleus
mRNA moves to a ribosome in the cytoplasm
ribosome assembles amino acids in the order coded by mRNA
forming a specific protein

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers made clear that DNA stays in the nucleus.

parts.prompt: Name the type of cell division that produces gametes.

markingPoints.text: meiosis

parts.examinerComment: Mitosis was a common wrong answer.

parts.prompt: Two plants that are both heterozygous for flower colour (Rr) are crossed. R (red) is dominant to r (white). {=4*k} offspring are produced. Calculate the expected number of white-flowered plants.

markingPoints.text: ratio of red to white is 3 : 1 / 1 in 4 are rr

parts.examinerComment: Expected numbers are rarely seen exactly in real crosses because fertilisation is random.

parts.prompt: A population of beetles lives on dark soil. Most beetles are dark brown, but a few are pale. Explain how natural selection keeps most of the beetles dark brown.

markingPoints.text: there is variation in colour
pale beetles are more easily seen by predators and eaten
dark beetles are more likely to survive and reproduce
pass on alleles for dark colour to offspring
frequency of the dark allele stays high

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used 'alleles' and 'reproduce' in the explanation.

parts.prompt: Describe how a farmer could use selective breeding to produce cattle with a high milk yield.

markingPoints.text: choose cows with the highest milk yield
breed with bulls whose mothers had high milk yield
select the best offspring and breed them
repeat over many generations

parts.examinerComment: Answers describing genetic modification were not credited.

parts.prompt: In a survey of {n} students, {k} could roll their tongue. Calculate the percentage of students who could roll their tongue.
parts.examinerComment: Tongue rolling is often given as an example of discontinuous variation.

parts.prompt: In a food chain, the primary consumers receive {a} kJ of energy and the secondary consumers receive {b} kJ. Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from the primary to the secondary consumers.

markingPoints.text: efficiency = energy transferred ÷ energy available × 100

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates inverted the fraction, giving a value over 100%.

parts.prompt: Explain why food chains usually have fewer than five trophic levels.

markingPoints.text: energy is lost at each trophic level
by respiration / as heat / movement / excretion / undigested material
not enough energy left to support another level

parts.examinerComment: Energy is not 'used up'; it is transferred to the environment.

parts.prompt: State the term for all the populations of different species living in the same area.

markingPoints.text: community

parts.examinerComment: 'Ecosystem' includes the non-living environment and was not accepted.

parts.prompt: Satellite images show that the area of a forest fell from {a} km² to {b} km² in ten years. Calculate the percentage decrease in the area of the forest.

markingPoints.text: decrease = {a} − {b} = {=a-b} km²

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates calculated this correctly.

parts.prompt: Describe methods used to conserve an endangered species.

markingPoints.text: protect habitats / set up reserves
captive breeding programmes
seed banks / sperm and egg banks
education
laws against hunting / trade
monitoring populations

parts.examinerComment: Answers should give named methods, not just 'protect them'.

parts.prompt: Explain how non-biodegradable plastics can harm aquatic organisms.

markingPoints.text: not broken down by decomposers so remain for a long time
animals become trapped / entangled
animals eat plastic, blocking the gut / causing starvation
small plastic particles pass along food chains

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained why plastic persists in the environment.

parts.prompt: Explain why biological washing powders remove stains better at 40 °C than at 15 °C.

markingPoints.text: washing powder contains enzymes such as proteases / lipases
40 °C is closer to the optimum temperature
more kinetic energy, more frequent collisions between enzyme and substrate
more enzyme–substrate complexes formed

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates wrongly said the enzymes are denatured at 15 °C.

parts.prompt: Describe how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.

markingPoints.text: human insulin gene cut out using restriction enzymes
leaving sticky ends
plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme
gene inserted into plasmid using DNA ligase
recombinant plasmid inserted into bacteria
bacteria multiply and express the gene / make insulin

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers described the steps in the correct sequence and named both enzymes.

parts.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing genetically modified crops.

markingPoints.text: advantage: higher yield / resistance to insect pests or herbicides
advantage: fewer pesticides needed / improved nutritional value
disadvantage: reduced biodiversity / genes may spread to wild plants
disadvantage: seeds may be expensive / possible health concerns

parts.examinerComment: A discussion needs both advantages and disadvantages.
